Contents/Part IV/Chapter 13
Chapter 13 · Spatial Intelligence for Intelligent Assistance

13.1Introduction

PDF p. 436· 1 min read

An intelligent assistant is a generalist embodied agent that shares the user’s own private, unstructured world and acts on the user’s behalf. Unlike the domain agents of the preceding chapters, which are optimized for a bounded operational envelope (a road network, a warehouse aisle, an operating theater), the assistant must function inside the open-ended geometry of a home, an office, or a sidewalk, in the continuous physical presence of the person it serves. Its defining spatial challenge is therefore not a new perception, reasoning, generation, or memory primitive: those capabilities are surveyed in Chapter 6 (perception), Chapter 7 (reasoning), Chapter 8 (generation), and Section 7.3.6 (retrieval- and memory-augmented spatial reasoning). The challenge here is rather to build and maintain a persistent, personalized, and queryable spatial-semantic model of the user’s environment, to ground human intent onto that model, and to act on it legibly and safely while a person occupies the same space.

Three properties separate the assistant from the embodied agents discussed elsewhere in this part. The environment is the user’s own, so the assistant cannot assume an engineered layout and must instead generalize across the long tail of real homes. It is also personalized: the same instruction (“tidy up,” “take me to the exit”) resolves to different geometric goals for different users, so the spatial model must absorb individual preference. And because the human is always co-present, otherwise routine motion becomes a social act that must be predictable, comfortable, and safe. These three demands (an unengineered space, an individual user, and a person sharing that space) recur across every regime in which the assistant operates.
